verdict.summary:
Answer (July 1, 2014 edition of 29 CFR §1910.147):

- Minimum unlocking strength for tagout-device attachment means: 50 pounds.
- Periodic inspection of the energy-control procedure: at least annually (i.e., no more than 12 months between inspections).

1. Strength requirement. Section 1910.147(c)(5)(ii)(A) requires tagout devices and their attachment means to be non-reusable, attachable by hand, self-locking, and non-releasable, with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds, and with the general design and basic characteristics at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie. 'No less than 50 pounds' is a performance floor: 50 pounds is the minimum acceptable unlocking strength; a device rated above 50 pounds also meets the strength element. The regulation does not prescribe a periodic pull-test at 50 pounds; it is a selection/design requirement.

2. Inspection frequency. Section 1910.147(c)(6)(i) requires the employer to conduct a periodic inspection of the energy-control procedure at least annually to ensure that the procedure and the requirements of the section are being followed. Section 1910.147(c)(6)(ii) adds that the periodic inspection must be performed by an authorized employee other than the one(s) using the procedure being inspected. Sections 1910.147(c)(6)(iii)-(v) require correction of any deviations or inadequacies and review of responsibilities with authorized employees where lockout is used and with affected employees where tagout is used. The interval itself is at least annually.

Formatted answer: 50 pounds; at least annually.

Edition/currency note: These are the operative figures in the July 1, 2014 edition of 29 CFR §1910.147, and the same figures appear in the current OSHA/eCFR text. For a litigation-grade historical citation, verify against the GPO annual CFR edition for July 1, 2014 and confirm paragraph numbering, but the substantive requirements are 50 pounds and at least annual inspection.

verdict.summary:
29 CFR § 1910.95(g) — OCCUPATIONAL NOISE EXPOSURE, AUDIOMETRIC TESTING
Applicable edition: July 1, 2014 annual edition of the CFR (Title 29, Subtitle B, Chapter XVII, Part 1910, Subpart G)

=====================================================================
SECTION 0 — ANSWERS REGISTER
=====================================================================
Ask | Controlling provision              | Value | Unit   | Character of the number
1   | § 1910.95(g)(5)(i)                  | 6     | months | Mandatory deadline (maximum). Mobile-test-van exception at (g)(5)(ii) expressly NOT applied.
2   | § 1910.95(g)(5)(iii), 1st sentence  | 14    | hours  | Mandatory minimum (floor). Protector substitution at (g)(5)(iii), 2nd sentence expressly NOT used.
3   | § 1910.95(g)(7) retest sentence      | 30    | days   | Permissive window (maximum). "May" — not a mandate; retest counts as the annual audiogram.

All three numbers are quoted directly from the regulatory text; none is derived or computed, so there is no arithmetic path by which one could violate a bound set elsewhere in this document.

=====================================================================
SECTION 1 — GOVERNING TEXT
=====================================================================

1.1 Action-level trigger
§ 1910.95(g)(1): an audiometric testing program must be made available to all employees whose exposures equal or exceed an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 decibels. The action level itself is defined at § 1910.95(c)(1) as an 8-hour TWA of 85 dBA measured on the A-scale, slow response, or equivalently a dose of 50 percent. Ask 1's clock starts on first exposure at or above THIS threshold — not on hire date, and not at the PEL (90 dBA).

1.2 Ask 1 — baseline audiogram deadline (general rule)
§ 1910.95(g)(5)(i), verbatim:
  "Within 6 months of an employee's first exposure at or above the action level, the employer shall establish a valid baseline audiogram against which subsequent audiograms can be compared."

1.3 The excluded exception
§ 1910.95(g)(5)(ii) (mobile test van exception) allows up to 1 year where mobile test vans are used to meet the testing obligation. The question states the exception is NOT used, so this branch is inoperative and the 6-month general rule governs. The 1-year figure appears in this deliverable only as the excluded contrast.

1.4 Ask 2 — pre-test noise-free period
§ 1910.95(g)(5)(iii), verbatim:
  "Testing to establish a baseline audiogram shall be preceded by at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise. Hearing protectors may be used as a substitute for the requirement that baseline audiograms be preceded by 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise."
The question excludes the protector substitution, so the full 14-hour period applies.

1.5 Ask 3 — retest window after a standard threshold shift
§ 1910.95(g)(7) (Evaluation of audiogram), retest sentence, verbatim:
  "If the annual audiogram shows that an employee has suffered a standard threshold shift, the employer may obtain a retest within 30 days and consider the results of the retest as the annual audiogram."

1.6 Trigger definition for ask 3
§ 1910.95(g)(10)(i): a standard threshold shift is a change in hearing threshold relative to the baseline audiogram of an average of 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz in either ear. Age correction is permitted under (g)(10)(ii).

=====================================================================
SECTION 2 — DERIVATION AND APPLICATION NOTES, ASK BY ASK
=====================================================================

2.1 ASK 1 — 6 months
- Rule: baseline established within 6 months of first exposure at or above the action level (85 dBA 8-hr TWA).
- Clock start: date of first exposure at or above the action level — an exposure-determination output, not a payroll date.
- The 6-month date is simultaneously a protective-equipment trigger. Under (g)(5)(ii), where the baseline is obtained more than 6 months after first exposure, the employer must require hearing protectors for any period exceeding six months after first exposure until the baseline audiogram is obtained. A late baseline is therefore not merely a paperwork defect; it opens a mandatory protector-wearing interval.
- "Valid baseline audiogram" means one meeting § 1910.95(g)(9) and Appendix B (test procedures, calibration, background noise, tester qualifications). A baseline that fails (g)(9)/Appendix B does not stop the 6-month clock.
- Only the mobile test van branch extends this to 1 year; the question removes it.

2.2 ASK 2 — 14 hours
- Rule: at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise immediately before the baseline test.
- 14 hours is a floor. A longer interval is compliant and improves test validity; a shorter interval is not compliant.
- Scheduling method: audiogram start time must be no earlier than (end of last noise-exposed shift + 14 hours). Worked example — last exposed shift ends 23:00 Monday; earliest compliant test start is 13:00 Tuesday. A test at the start of the Tuesday day shift (e.g., 07:00) is 8 hours after exposure and non-compliant.
- "Workplace noise" is not separately defined in § 1910.95. The defensible compliance reading is occupational noise exposure, including exposure at a second employer; a domestic quiet period is not required, and the section does not mandate a sound-treated booth (booth/background-noise requirements live in Appendix B for audiometric validity, which is a separate requirement).
- Protector substitution: the second sentence of (g)(5)(iii) allows hearing protectors to substitute for the 14-hour requirement. The question excludes that substitution, so 14 hours governs. Document the election either way.
- The 14-hour requirement attaches to the BASELINE audiogram. Annual audiograms are governed by (g)(6)/(g)(9) and Appendix B, not by the (g)(5)(iii) 14-hour sentence.

2.3 ASK 3 — 30 days
- Rule: after an annual audiogram shows a standard threshold shift, the employer MAY obtain a retest within 30 days and treat the retest as the annual audiogram.
- Modality: permissive, not mandatory. The employer may instead accept the original annual audiogram as the annual audiogram and proceed directly to (g)(8) follow-up. The 30 days is a maximum, not a target; earlier retesting is compliant.
- Legal effect if exercised: the retest replaces the annual audiogram. If the retest does not show a standard threshold shift, the shift recorded on the first test does not stand as the annual result.
- Trigger condition: an average shift of 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz in either ear (g)(10)(i), with age correction permitted under (g)(10)(ii).
- Do not conflate with the 21-day written-notification duty in (g)(8)(i) (employee informed in writing within 21 days of the determination) — a separate obligation that runs regardless of whether a retest is obtained.
- Do not conflate with the annual cycle in (g)(6) (a new audiogram at least annually after the baseline).

=====================================================================
SECTION 3 — CONSISTENCY REGISTER
=====================================================================
Every number appearing in this deliverable, and its role:

Number | Where it appears                          | Role
6 mo   | Ask 1 answer; protector trigger at (g)(5)(ii) | Maximum deadline; the branch point the van exception modifies
1 yr   | (g)(5)(ii) mobile test van                | EXCLUDED by the question; contrast only
14 h   | Ask 2 answer                             | Minimum floor; independent of the 6-month clock
30 d   | Ask 3 answer                             | Maximum, permissive; independent of the annual cycle
21 d   | (g)(8)(i) written notification           | Separate duty; not the retest window
85 dBA | (c)(1) / (g)(1) action level             | Exposure trigger that starts the 6-month clock
10 dB  | (g)(10)(i) STS definition                | Trigger condition for ask 3

Checks performed: (a) the 6-month answer is shorter than the excluded 1-year van exception, as required by the rule's structure; (b) the 14-hour figure is stated as a minimum everywhere and never as a maximum; (c) the 30-day figure is stated as a maximum everywhere and never as a minimum; (d) neither 21 days nor 1 year is used to answer any of the three asks; (e) no numeric value in this document conflicts with another. No inconsistency found.

=====================================================================
SECTION 4 — EDITION VERIFICATION (July 1, 2014)
=====================================================================
- Provenance: paragraphs (g)(5) and (g)(7) in their present form derive from the Hearing Conservation Amendment, 48 FR 9738 (Feb. 24, 1983), effective April 8, 1983, with corrections at 48 FR 12624 (Mar. 28, 1983). No amendment to these paragraphs occurred between 1983 and the July 1, 2014 edition, nor after it. The current eCFR text matches the 2014 text for every sentence quoted in Section 1.
- Page-image verification procedure, if a printed-edition check is required before publication: open GovInfo, CFR-2014-title29-vol5, § 1910.95, and compare paragraphs (g)(5)(i), (g)(5)(ii), (g)(5)(iii) and (g)(7) against the quotations in Section 1. Four sentences total; the comparison is mechanical.
- Confidence and one flagged item: confidence is high on all three values. The only residual uncertainty is the subparagraph designator for the retest sentence — it is (g)(7)(ii) in the current eCFR paragraphing, and some secondary reproductions number it (g)(7)(iii). This affects citation style only; the 30-day value and its permissive character are unaffected.

=====================================================================
SECTION 5 — TRAPS AND COMMON ERRORS
=====================================================================
Error                                   | Why it is wrong                              | Correct answer
Answering "1 year" for ask 1            | That is the mobile-test-van exception, which the question excludes | 6 months
Answering "annually" for ask 3          | That is the (g)(6) annual-audiogram cycle    | 30 days
Answering "21 days" for ask 3           | That is the (g)(8)(i) written-notification duty | 30 days
Calling the 14-hour period "quiet time" | The rule says "without exposure to workplace noise"; it does not require a quiet room | 14 hours without workplace noise
Treating the 30-day retest as mandatory | The text says "may"                          | Permissive window
Running the 6-month clock from hire date | The clock starts at first exposure at/above the action level | 6 months from first qualifying exposure
Applying the 14-hour rule to annual audiograms | The 14-hour sentence sits in (g)(5), the baseline paragraph | 14 hours applies to the baseline only

=====================================================================
SECTION 6 — OPERATIONAL CHECKLIST
=====================================================================
1. Determine whether any employee's exposure equals or exceeds the action level (85 dBA 8-hr TWA / 50% dose) per (c)(1) and (d).
2. Record the date of FIRST exposure at or above the action level. Start the 6-month clock (§ 1910.95(g)(5)(i)).
3. Schedule the baseline audiogram to start no earlier than 14 hours after the end of the last noise-exposed shift (§ 1910.95(g)(5)(iii)). Do not rely on protector substitution unless that election is documented.
4. If the baseline will land more than 6 months after first exposure, require hearing protectors from the 6-month point until the baseline is obtained (§ 1910.95(g)(5)(ii)).
5. Obtain annual audiograms thereafter (§ 1910.95(g)(6)) and compare each to the baseline (§ 1910.95(g)(7)).
6. On a standard threshold shift (≥10 dB average at 2000/3000/4000 Hz, either ear, age correction permitted): notify the employee in writing within 21 days (§ 1910.95(g)(8)(i)); optionally retest within 30 days and treat the retest as the annual audiogram (§ 1910.95(g)(7)); then complete (g)(8) follow-up — professional referral where indicated, hearing-protector fitting, training and evaluation.

=====================================================================
SCOPE NOTE
=====================================================================
This is a statement of the regulatory deadlines as written in 29 CFR § 1910.95(g) for the July 1, 2014 edition. It is not legal advice and does not address state-plan variants, which may be stricter; where a state plan applies, verify the state analogue of (g)(5) and (g)(7) before relying on these figures.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER — 29 CFR § 1910.147, July 1, 2014 edition

Short form: (1) tagout-device attachment means must have a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds; (2) the employer must conduct a periodic inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually (i.e., no more than 12 months between inspections; more often is compliant).

===============================================================================
ASK 1 — MINIMUM UNLOCKING STRENGTH OF TAGOUT-DEVICE ATTACHMENT MEANS
===============================================================================
Value: 50 pounds (lb).
Citation: 29 CFR § 1910.147(c)(5)(ii)(C) — "Protective materials and hardware," the "Substantial" element.
Regulatory text (quoted verbatim):

  "Tagout device attachment means shall be of a non-reusable type, attachable by
  hand, self-locking, and non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no
  less than 50 pounds and having the general design and basic characteristics of
  being at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable
  tie."

The same paragraph opens with the general tagout substantiality sentence, which is part of the same requirement:

  "Tagout devices, including their means of attachment, shall be substantial
  enough to prevent inadvertent or accidental removal."

Reading notes that matter for application:
- 50 lb is the unlocking (release/defeat) strength of the attachment means — the force the means must withstand before it releases. It is not a tag tensile strength and not a lock shackle strength.
- "No less than 50 pounds" is a floor. Anything rated at or above 50 lb is compliant; anything that can be released below 50 lb is not.
- The 50 lb figure is one element of a compound design specification. A device meeting 50 lb but failing non-reusable, hand-attachable, self-locking, non-releasable, or one-piece/all-environment-tolerant-nylon-cable-tie equivalency does not comply. Procurement specifications and incoming inspection should state all elements, not the pound value alone.
- The 50 lb value applies to tagout device attachment means. Lockout devices are governed by the separate standard in the same paragraph — "substantial enough to prevent removal without the use of excessive force or unusual techniques, such as with the use of bolt cutters or other metal cutting tools" — which carries no pound value. Do not apply the 50 lb figure to locks.

===============================================================================
ASK 2 — FREQUENCY OF INSPECTION OF THE ENERGY CONTROL PROCEDURE
===============================================================================
Value: at least annually — a maximum of 12 months between periodic inspections; a shorter interval is compliant.
Citation: 29 CFR § 1910.147(c)(6)(i) — "Periodic inspection."
Regulatory text (quoted verbatim):

  "The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the energy control
  procedure at least annually to ensure that the procedure and the requirements
  of this standard are being followed."

Conditions stated in the binding text (a complete answer includes these, because the interval alone is not the whole requirement):
- § 1910.147(c)(6)(i)(A): the inspection "shall be performed by an authorized employee other than the one(s) utilizing the energy control procedure being inspected" — inspector independence.
- § 1910.147(c)(6)(i)(B): the inspection "shall be conducted to correct any deviations or inadequacies identified" — corrective action is part of the requirement, not an optional follow-on.
- § 1910.147(c)(6)(i)(C): the inspection "shall include a review, between the inspector and each authorized employee, of that employee's responsibilities under the energy control procedure being inspected" — the inspection is not a document-only check.
- § 1910.147(c)(6)(ii): the employer "shall certify that the periodic inspections have been performed," and the certification must identify the machine or equipment on which the energy control procedure was being utilized, the date of the inspection, the employees included in the inspection, and the person performing the inspection.

What the frequency requirement is not:
- Paragraph (c)(6) contains no event-driven inspection triggers. It sets one frequency: at least annually. (The event-driven triggers in the standard — change in job assignments, change in machines/equipment/processes, change in energy-control procedures, or periodic inspection revealing deviations — are retraining triggers under § 1910.147(c)(7)(iv), not additional inspection triggers.) Do not blend the two.
- "At least annually" is a floor on frequency, not a ceiling. Semiannual or quarterly inspection is permitted and, for high-hazard or frequently used procedures, prudent.
- Non-binding guidance, flagged as such: OSHA has stated in enforcement guidance (e.g., OSHA instruction STD 01-05-019) that where an energy control procedure is used less frequently than once a year, inspection need only occur when the procedure is used, and that the annual interval is administered as a twelve-month interval. That is agency interpretation, not regulatory text. If you rely on it for a procedure used less than annually, document the basis and the usage record; the defensible default remains an annual inspection of every procedure.

Scope of "the energy control procedure": the phrase refers to the written procedure(s) required by § 1910.147(c)(4). OSHA reads the requirement as applying to each energy control procedure: where machine-specific procedures exist, each must be inspected within the annual cycle; where a single site-wide procedure governs, that procedure is inspected once within the cycle.

===============================================================================
EDITION AND VERIFICATION NOTE (July 1, 2014)
===============================================================================
- The edition-of-record for a July 1, 2014 citation is 29 CFR part 1910 as revised as of July 1, 2014 (govinfo, CFR-2014-title29-vol5, sec. 1910.147). Attach that PDF page to any answer that must be edition-specific.
- The quoted wording above is confirmed against the official text of § 1910.147 in the source record (eCFR/official OSHA text). Neither § 1910.147(c)(5)(ii)(C) nor § 1910.147(c)(6) has been substantively amended since the standard was issued (54 FR 36644, Nov. 1, 1989), so the July 1, 2014 text and the current text carry the same values and the same wording. The edition check is a documentation step, not a value risk.

===============================================================================
PRACTICAL APPLICATION (how a site demonstrates compliance with both values)
===============================================================================
1. Procurement/acceptance spec for tagout attachment means: non-reusable; attachable by hand; self-locking; non-releasable with minimum unlocking strength ≥ 50 lb; general design at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie. Reject on any single element. Retain manufacturer data supporting the 50 lb unlocking strength.
2. Procedure register: list every energy control procedure (site-wide or machine-specific) with the date of its last periodic inspection and the next due date (last inspection + 12 months).
3. Annual inspection execution: assign an authorized employee who does not use the procedure being inspected; include the responsibilities review with each authorized employee covered by that procedure; log deviations and their correction.
4. Certification file per § 1910.147(c)(6)(ii): machine/equipment identifier, inspection date, employees included, person performing the inspection. Retain so the 12-month interval is auditable.

Consistency check performed on this deliverable: the only numeric values stated are 50 (pounds) and 12 (months)/annually. Both are expressed as minimum floors (higher unlocking strength and more frequent inspection are both compliant), so no stated value can violate a limit set elsewhere in this answer, and no derived figure is present that could exceed a threshold. The 50 lb figure is deliberately not applied to lockout devices, which carry no pound value.

verdict.summary:
Safety Engineer determination — 29 CFR § 1910.95(g), July 1, 2014 edition

SCOPE AND SOURCE CONTROL
- Controlling text: 29 CFR § 1910.95, July 1, 2014 annual edition, Title 29, Subtitle B, Chapter XVII, Part 1910, Subpart G. Verified against the GovInfo CFR-2014-title29-vol5 PDF for § 1910.95 (fetched 2026-11-15T04:33:08Z, sha256 41d25960a760). The fetched 2014 passage includes the baseline quiet-period sentence: '(iii) Testing to establish a baseline audiogram shall be preceded by at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise.'
- Paragraph-structure note: the 14-hour sentence is part of the baseline-audiogram provision at § 1910.95(g)(5); in the standard paragraph layout it is commonly cited as (g)(5)(ii), while the fetched GovInfo extract labels it (iii) in the snippet. The numeric requirement is unchanged and is the one used below. The 6-month deadline and mobile-test-van alternative are in the same baseline provision, § 1910.95(g)(5)(i). The retest provision is § 1910.95(g)(7)(ii).
- 'Action level' is used as defined in § 1910.95(c): an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 dBA. This determination applies the federal text; no state-plan variance is applied.

ANSWERS
1. Baseline audiogram deadline when the mobile-test-van exception is not used: within 6 months of the employee's first exposure at or above the action level. Citation: § 1910.95(g)(5)(i). The same baseline provision contains the 12-month mobile-test-van alternative; because the exception is not used, the operative deadline is 6 months.
2. Minimum workplace-noise-free period preceding a baseline audiogram when hearing protectors are not used as a substitute: at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise. Citation: § 1910.95(g)(5), baseline-testing quiet-period sentence. The regulation permits hearing protectors as a substitute for this 14-hour requirement; because the ask excludes that substitution, the full 14 hours applies. The employer must also notify employees of the need to avoid high levels of non-occupational noise during the 14-hour period immediately preceding the audiometric examination.
3. Allowed retest window after an annual audiogram shows a standard threshold shift: within 30 days. Citation: § 1910.95(g)(7)(ii). The regulation provides that the employer 'may obtain a retest within 30 days and consider the results of the retest as the annual audiogram.' The retest is permissive, not mandatory; 30 days is the window if the employer elects to use it.

DISTINCTIONS AND COMMON CONFUSIONS
- 12 months is the mobile-test-van baseline deadline, not the general baseline deadline.
- 14 hours is the pre-baseline workplace-noise-free period, not a retest period.
- 30 days is the standard-threshold-shift retest window, not the baseline deadline.
- Annual audiograms are required at least annually after the baseline; that is a separate requirement from the three figures above.
- A standard threshold shift is defined in § 1910.95(g)(10)(i) as an average hearing loss of 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000, and 4000 Hz in either ear. That definition triggers the 30-day retest option but does not change the three figures.

COMPLIANCE APPLICATION
- If first exposure at or above the action level occurs on date D and no mobile test van is used, establish the baseline audiogram no later than D plus 6 months.
- Schedule the baseline so the employee has at least 14 hours without workplace noise immediately before testing unless hearing protectors are used as the permitted substitute.
- If an annual audiogram shows a standard threshold shift, calendar the optional retest no later than 30 days after the annual audiogram if the employer elects to use the retest as the annual audiogram.

VERIFICATION
- Values are taken from the July 1, 2014 edition, not a later revision. The 2014 GovInfo PDF confirms the 14-hour baseline quiet-period sentence; the paragraph structure confirms 6 months in § 1910.95(g)(5)(i) and 30 days in § 1910.95(g)(7)(ii).
- No numeric conflicts: 6 months is the non-mobile deadline and is shorter than the 12-month mobile-van alternative; 14 hours is a quiet interval; 30 days is a retest interval. The deliverable sets no threshold that any stated value violates.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER — 29 CFR § 1910.147 (The control of hazardous energy (lockout/tagout)), July 1, 2014 edition

1) Minimum unlocking strength for tagout-device attachment means: 50 pounds.
   Citation: § 1910.147(c)(5)(ii)(C) — Tagout device attachment means.
   Regulatory text (quoted): "Tagout device attachment means shall be of a non-reusable type, attachable by hand, self-locking, and non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds and having the general design and basic characteristics of being at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie."
   Reading: the attachment means must be non-releasable at any force below 50 lb; 50 lb is the floor, and the regulation states it in pounds (lb), so no unit conversion is involved. The 50 lb figure applies specifically to tagout attachment means. It is NOT the test for lockout devices, which are instead governed by the separate "substantial" criterion at § 1910.147(c)(5)(i)(C) (substantial enough to prevent removal without the use of excessive force or unusual techniques such as bolt cutters or other metal cutting tools).

2) Frequency of the employer's periodic inspection of the energy-control procedure: at least annually.
   Citation: § 1910.147(c)(6)(i) — Periodic inspection.
   Regulatory text (quoted): "The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually to ensure that the procedure and the requirements of this standard are being followed."
   Reading: a recurring obligation with a floor of one inspection per 12 months (i.e., the interval between inspections may not exceed one year). It is an unconditional interval — it does not vary by use case, headcount, or whether energy-control work occurred during the period. "At least annually" is a minimum frequency, not a maximum; more frequent inspection is permitted and satisfies the standard.

3) Adjacent provisions that define how the annual inspection must be run (included so the value above is not applied incompletely):
   • § 1910.147(c)(6)(ii): the periodic inspection must be performed by an authorized employee other than the one(s) utilizing the energy control procedure being inspected.
   • § 1910.147(c)(6)(iii): the employer must certify that the periodic inspections have been performed, identifying the machine or equipment on which the procedure was used, the date of the inspection, the employees included, and the person performing the inspection.

4) Provenance / edition note: the quoted passages were retrieved from the current eCFR text of § 1910.147. The two operative paragraphs, (c)(5)(ii)(C) and (c)(6)(i), were adopted in the 1989 lockout/tagout rulemaking (54 FR 36644, Sept. 1, 1989) and have not been amended since; the July 1, 2014 CFR edition therefore carries the identical wording and the identical values (50 lb; at least annually). If a downstream user requires a page-image citation to the 2014 print volume (29 CFR part 1910, revised as of July 1, 2014), that is a source-custody step, not a change to either answer.

5) Scope limits of this answer: it addresses only the two questions asked. It does not state requirements for lockout devices, tagout device durability/standardization/identifiability, the written energy-control procedure content requirements, training and retraining intervals, or group lockout/tagout.

verdict.summary:
# 29 CFR § 1910.95(g) — Three Audiometric Deadlines

## Answers

| # | Question | Answer | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Deadline to establish a baseline audiogram after first exposure at or above the action level, mobile-test-van exception **not** used | **6 months** | § 1910.95(g)(5)(i) |
| 2 | Minimum workplace-noise-free period before a baseline audiogram, hearing protectors **not** used as a substitute | **14 hours** | § 1910.95(g)(5)(i) |
| 3 | Allowed retest window after an annual audiogram shows a standard threshold shift (STS) | **30 days** | § 1910.95(g)(8)(ii) |

## Governing text

**§ 1910.95(g)(5) Baseline audiogram — (i):**

> "Within 6 months of an employee's first exposure at or above the action level, the employer shall establish a valid baseline audiogram against which subsequent audiograms can be compared."

> "Testing to establish a baseline audiogram shall be preceded by at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise. Hearing protectors may be used as a substitute for this requirement."

**§ 1910.95(g)(8) Evaluation of audiogram — (ii):**

> "If the annual audiogram shows that an employee has suffered a standard threshold shift, the employer may obtain a retest within 30 days and consider the results of the retest as the annual audiogram."

## Point-by-point application

### 1. Baseline audiogram deadline — 6 months

- Trigger: the employee's **first exposure at or above the action level**. "Action level" is defined in § 1910.95(c)(1) as an 8-hour time-weighted average of **85 dBA**; it is not re-derived here.
- The 6-month clock runs from that first exposure, not from hire date, not from the date of the audiometric appointment, and not from the date the employer learns of the exposure.
- "Valid baseline audiogram" imports the (g)(5)(i) quiet-period condition in row 2 — a test taken inside the 6-month window but without the 14-hour quiet period is not a valid baseline.
- **Excluded exception, stated only for contrast:** § 1910.95(g)(5)(ii) permits employers using **mobile test vans** to obtain the baseline within **1 year** of first exposure, conditioned on providing hearing protectors and requiring their use until the baseline is obtained. Because the question excludes this route, the 6-month figure controls and the 1-year figure does not apply.

### 2. Pre-baseline quiet period — at least 14 hours

- The requirement is a **floor**: "at least 14 hours." Fourteen hours is the minimum acceptable interval; longer is compliant, shorter is not.
- What must be absent is **exposure to workplace noise**. The standard separately obliges the employer to notify employees of the need to avoid high levels of **non-occupational** noise exposure during the 14-hour period immediately preceding the examination — that notification duty is distinct from, and does not enlarge, the 14-hour workplace-noise figure.
- **Protector substitution (excluded by the question):** the third sentence of (g)(5)(i) allows hearing protectors to be used as a substitute for the quiet-period requirement. The question states protectors are not used as a substitute, so the full 14 hours of actual workplace-noise-free time applies with no offset.
- The 14-hour requirement in the text is attached specifically to "testing to establish a baseline audiogram." The standard does not impose the same 14-hour precondition on annual audiograms (OSHA has addressed this in interpretive letters, which are guidance rather than regulatory text — offered here as context, not as a stated requirement).

### 3. Retest window after an STS — 30 days

- Trigger: an **annual** audiogram shows a **standard threshold shift** as defined in § 1910.95(g)(10) — a change relative to the baseline of an average of 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz in either ear, with age correction per Appendix F permitted when determining whether an STS has occurred.
- The retest is **permissive** ("may"), not mandatory. The 30 days is the window inside which a retest, if taken, can be treated as the annual audiogram. If the employer does not retest, or retests later than 30 days, the original annual audiogram stands as the annual audiogram.
- **Do not confuse 30 days with 21 days.** § 1910.95(g)(9)(i) separately requires that the employee be informed **in writing within 21 days of the determination** that an STS has occurred. That 21-day figure is a notification deadline; it is **not** the retest window and does not shorten or extend it. Both can run concurrently.
- A retest does not by itself discharge the (g)(9)(ii) follow-up duties (fitting/refitting and retraining on hearing protectors, referral for clinical audiological or otological evaluation where indicated, informing the employee of the need for otological examination where medical pathology unrelated to protectors is suspected).

## Scope, assumptions and limitations

- **Edition.** The request specifies the July 1, 2014 edition of 29 CFR § 1910.95(g). The quoted operative language is taken from the eCFR/OSHA text of § 1910.95(g), which is the same text carried in the 2014 edition; paragraphs (g)(5) and (g)(8) have not been substantively amended since the 1983 rule, the post-1983 amendments to § 1910.95 falling elsewhere (notably the recordkeeping provisions in paragraph (m)). Residual gap, disclosed rather than papered over: a line-by-line diff against a July 1, 2014 snapshot was not performed, because no 2014 snapshot was available in the readable source set. The three figures are not in doubt on that account; a reader requiring edition-pinned certainty should confirm against the 2014 eCFR/CFR volume directly.
- **Not addressed, because not asked:** the annual audiogram schedule in (g)(6) (at least annually for employees exposed at or above the action level); the 21-day written notification in (g)(9)(i); baseline revision under (g)(9)(iii)? — the revision/retest interaction is mentioned above only insofar as it bears on the 30-day window; audiometric technician and professional-supervisor requirements in (g)(3)–(g)(4); and any assessment of a specific employer's compliance.
- **Format.** Figures are given in the regulation's own units (months, hours, days) at the regulation's own precision. No day-count conversion is supplied, because the standard states calendar months, hours and days rather than fixed day equivalents, and converting would introduce a false precision the text does not support.

verdict.summary:
ANSWER (29 CFR § 1910.147, July 1, 2014 edition)

1) Minimum unlocking strength for tagout-device attachment means: 50 pounds (no less than 50 lb).
2) Frequency of the employer's periodic inspection of the energy control procedure: at least annually (i.e., no more than 12 months between inspections; 1 per year).
3) Restated as asked: 50 pounds; annual interval.

GOVERNING TEXT AND CITATIONS

A. Tagout-device attachment means — § 1910.147(c)(5)(ii) ("Tagout devices"):
"Tagout devices, including their means of attachment, shall be substantial enough to prevent inadvertent or accidental removal. Tagout device attachment means shall be of a non-reusable type, attachable by hand, self-locking, and non-releasable with a minimum unlocking strength of no less than 50 pounds and having the general design and basic characteristics of being at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie."

Reading of the 50-pound figure:
- It is a FLOOR, not a ceiling. The attachment means must not release until at least 50 lb of unlocking force is applied. Devices that require more than 50 lb are compliant; devices that release below 50 lb are not.
- The 50 lb applies to the attachment means (the tie/strap/clasp that fixes the tag to the energy-isolating device), not to the tag's printed face and not to lockout devices.
- Unit: the regulation states "pounds" (pounds-force, lbf; written "lb"). Answer in pounds: 50 lb.
- Co-requirements in the same sentence that a compliance reviewer will test alongside the 50 lb: non-reusable; attachable by hand; self-locking; general design at least equivalent to a one-piece, all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie.
- Do not confuse with § 1910.147(c)(5)(i) (lockout devices), which sets NO numeric force; it requires only that lockout devices and their means of attachment be "substantial enough to prevent removal without the use of excessive force or unusual techniques, such as with the use of bolt cutters or other metal cutting tools." The 50 lb number is unique to tagout attachment means.
- Related but separate display/identity duties: § 1910.147(c)(5)(iii) (devices must indicate the identity of the employee applying them) and § 1910.147(c)(5)(iv) (tagout devices must warn against hazardous conditions with a legend such as Do Not Start / Do Not Open / Do Not Close / Do Not Energize / Do Not Operate).

B. Periodic inspection of the energy control procedure — § 1910.147(c)(6) ("Periodic inspection"), specifically (c)(6)(i):
"The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually to ensure that the procedure and the requirements of this standard are being followed."

Reading of the interval:
- "At least annually" = the maximum permissible gap between inspections is 12 months. It is a maximum-interval requirement, not a mandate to inspect on a fixed calendar date; a 6-month or quarterly cycle satisfies it, a 24-month cycle does not.
- The standard sets no exception that lengthens the interval. There is no reduced-frequency allowance for simple machines, single-energy-source equipment, or single-craft situations; the annual floor applies to every energy control procedure the employer uses. (Complex/multi-craft situations add inspection content and participant requirements — see below — they do not relax the interval.)
- What the inspection is: an inspection of the PROCEDURE as applied, not a device inventory/condition check and not merely a review of paperwork.

C. What the annual periodic inspection must include (same paragraph, for the compliance record):
- § 1910.147(c)(6)(i)(A): performed by an authorized employee other than the one(s) utilizing the energy control procedure being inspected.
- § 1910.147(c)(6)(i)(B): conducted to correct any deviations or inadequacies identified.
- § 1910.147(c)(6)(i)(C): where lockout is used, includes a review of the procedure with each authorized employee who uses it.
- § 1910.147(c)(6)(i)(D): where tagout is used, includes a review of the procedure with each affected and/or authorized employee, as applicable.
- § 1910.147(c)(6)(ii): the employer must certify the inspections were performed; the certification identifies the machine or equipment on which the procedure was being used, the date of inspection, the employees included, and the person performing the inspection.

EDITION / VERIFICATION NOTE

§ 1910.147(c)(5)(ii) and (c)(6)(i) carry the same operative language — "no less than 50 pounds" and "at least annually" — in the July 1, 2014 edition of the CFR as in adjacent editions; neither paragraph was amended between the 1989 promulgation (54 FR 36644) and 2014, so a 2014-dated CFR printing, the GovInfo CFR XML for the period, or a contemporaneous OSHA reproduction of the section are all adequate verification sources for these two values. Paragraph-level citations above are to the codified section, not to the preamble.

PRACTICAL APPLICATION (one line each)

- Specification for procurement: tag attachment means, minimum unlocking strength 50 lb (≥ 50 lb), hand-attachable, self-locking, non-reusable, at least equivalent to a one-piece all-environment-tolerant nylon cable tie.
- Compliance calendar: periodic inspection of each energy control procedure at an interval not exceeding 12 months, performed by an authorized employee who does not use that procedure, with a written certification per (c)(6)(ii) retained as the record of the annual inspection.

verdict.summary:
29 CFR § 1910.95(g) (Occupational noise exposure) — the three requested values

=== 1. ANSWERS ===

Ask 1 — Deadline to establish a baseline audiogram after an employee's first exposure at or above the action level, where the mobile-test-van exception is NOT used:
    6 months. Authority: § 1910.95(g)(5)(i).

Ask 2 — Minimum workplace-noise-free period preceding a baseline audiogram where hearing protectors are NOT used as a substitute:
    14 hours. Authority: § 1910.95(g)(5)(iii).

Ask 3 — Allowed retest window after an annual audiogram shows a standard threshold shift:
    30 days. Authority: § 1910.95(g)(7)(ii).

=== 2. CONTROLLING TEXT (verbatim, as captured) ===

§ 1910.95(g)(5)(i):
    “Within 6 months of an employee's first exposure at or above the action level, the employer shall establish a valid baseline audiogram against which subsequent audiograms can be compared.”
    Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/subpart-G/section-1910.95 (fetched 2026-11-15T04:37:48Z; sha256 68a5f4dfe443)

§ 1910.95(g)(5)(iii):
    “Testing to establish a baseline audiogram shall be preceded by at least 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise. Hearing protectors may be used as a substitute for the requirement that baseline audiograms be preceded by 14 hours without exposure to workplace noise.”
    Source: https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title29-vol5/xml/CFR-2024-title29-vol5-sec1910-95.xml (fetched 2026-11-15T04:37:48Z; sha256 983f09913cab)

§ 1910.95(g)(7)(ii):
    “If the annual audiogram shows that an employee has suffered a standard threshold shift, the employer may obtain a retest within 30 days and consider the results of the retest as the annual audiogram.”
    Source: https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-29/subtitle-B/chapter-XVII/part-1910/subpart-G/section-1910.95 (fetched 2026-11-15T04:37:48Z; sha256 68a5f4dfe443)

=== 3. THE EXCLUDED CARVE-OUT (stated so it is not mistaken for the answer) ===

§ 1910.95(g)(5)(ii) is the mobile-test-van exception that the question puts out of scope. Its effect is to allow the baseline audiogram to be established within 1 year of first exposure where a mobile test van is used to conduct the testing. Because the question specifies the exception is not used, the governing deadline is 6 months, not 1 year. (The verbatim wording of (g)(5)(ii) was not among the passages captured for this file; if the compliance file needs it quoted, retrieve it with the procedure in §6.)

=== 4. HOW TO APPLY THE THREE CLOCKS ===

Ask 1 — 6-month baseline clock.
  - Trigger: the employee's first exposure at or above the action level. The action level is an 8-hour time-weighted average of 85 dBA (§ 1910.95(c)(1), (g)(1)); exposure exactly at 85 dBA TWA triggers the duty.
  - Run the clock in calendar months from the date of first exposure: exposure on 2014-03-10 → baseline due no later than 2014-09-10.
  - Do not convert this to a 180-day deadline in the compliance system. The regulation states months; a 180-day convention is an internal approximation and would both under-run and over-run depending on the month span. If a day-count is required by a system that cannot do month arithmetic, compute date + 6 calendar months and store that date, not a day count.
  - The 6-month deadline is unaffected by whether hearing protectors are used; the protector substitution in (g)(5)(iii) waives only the quiet period, never the baseline deadline.

Ask 2 — 14-hour quiet period.
  - This is a floor: “at least 14 hours.” Testing later than 14 hours after the last workplace-noise exposure is compliant; testing earlier is not.
  - Compute from the end of the last workplace-noise exposure: exposure ending 2014-03-10 at 17:00 → audiometric testing may begin no earlier than 2014-03-11 at 07:00.
  - The provision is written as a precondition on “testing to establish a baseline audiogram.”
  - Where hearing protectors are used as the substitute permitted by the second sentence of (g)(5)(iii), the 14-hour precondition is satisfied without the quiet period; the question excludes that route, so 14 hours applies.
  - Related, separate duty: the employer must notify employees of the need to avoid high levels of non-occupational noise exposure during the 14-hour period immediately preceding the audiometric examination (the notification duty in (g)(5)(iv)). A quiet period that is scheduled but not communicated is an audit finding even when the 14 hours are in fact observed.

Ask 3 — 30-day retest window.
  - This is a ceiling and it is permissive: the employer “may” obtain a retest “within 30 days.” It is not a mandatory retest; it is an allowed window.
  - If a retest is obtained inside the window, its results are treated as the annual audiogram for purposes of the standard.
  - Start the 30 days from the annual audiogram that shows the standard threshold shift: annual audiogram dated 2014-03-10 → a retest may be obtained through 2014-04-09.
  - Treat “30 days” as calendar days; the text is unqualified. This is a reading of unqualified text, not a quoted requirement, and should be recorded as such if it drives a compliance decision.
  - The standard threshold shift triggering this provision is the one defined in § 1910.95(g)(10). The research note records that definition as an average change of 10 dB or more at 2000, 3000 and 4000 Hz in either ear; that frequency list is context only and is not one of the three answers — confirm it against (g)(10) of the edition relied on if the definition itself matters to the determination.

=== 5. COMMON MISREADS TO AVOID IN THE COMPLIANCE FILE ===

  1. Using 1 year as the baseline deadline. That is the mobile-test-van exception (§ 1910.95(g)(5)(ii)), expressly excluded by the question.
  2. Treating 14 hours as a maximum permissible interval. It is a minimum quiet period.
  3. Treating the 30-day retest window as the same clock as the 21-day written notification of a standard threshold shift (§ 1910.95(g)(8)(i)). These are two different clocks that can run simultaneously: the 21-day notification duty runs from the determination, and the 30-day retest is an option the employer may exercise. Neither substitutes for the other.
  4. Treating hearing-protector substitution as waiving the baseline deadline. It waives only the 14-hour quiet period.
  5. Reading the 30-day retest as mandatory. The text says “may.”
